USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep existing Section 301 tariffs in place and continue intensive talks aimed at a written, enforceable agreement on IP, forced tech transfer, subsidies, and currency—not a purchases-only package. Do not raise List 3 from 10% to 25% while Lighthizer and Liu He are still working continuously, and do not roll tariffs back or trade away the Huawei/Meng criminal track as a concession. If Beijing will not accept unilateral, proportional snap-back enforcement, walk rather than sign a weak MOU.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is mildly negative (opportunity, not danger) because US leverage is working and the US real economy is not in a trade-war crisis. Combined coverage is already ~$250B of Chinese imports (Lists 1–3), the scheduled List 3 hike to 25% remains a live threat after the Feb 24 delay, and China is the side showing clearer stress: official manufacturing PMI contracted to 49.4 in December (first contraction in over two years), December exports fell 4.4% and imports 7.6%, 2018 GDP slowed to 6.6% with Q4 at 6.4%, and Beijing is already easing. US consumer sentiment recovered to 98.4 in March, VIX is 13.41, and CPI is contained; industrial production is only modestly softer. That is leverage terrain, not existential threat. The offset that keeps the reading from a deeper opportunity is real farm-belt damage: China’s matching retaliation hit soybeans and other ag; USDA’s Johansson (Feb 2019) said China soy purchases plummeted ~90%/22 million tons, China fell from the top US ag market to fifth, and ~25 million metric tons of soybeans were expected to go unsold, with ~$7.9B in farmer losses. IMPCH also dropped sharply into early 2019, so bilateral goods flows are already disrupted. Action should stay at negotiate (0) rather than escalate or concede because the talks themselves are the binding constraint as of mid-March: Lighthizer told Senate Finance on March 12 that “major issues” remain, success cannot be predicted, and nothing is done until everything is done—especially enforcement and how far tariffs would come off. Hawks in both parties (Schumer, Grassley, Ways and Means) have already warned against a purchase-heavy “half deal.” Hiking tariffs now would likely collapse a still-live channel after Trump just suspended the March 1 hike; rolling them back or committing purchases without structural/enforcement text would spend the leverage the 301 campaign created. Huawei/Meng (DOJ charges Jan 28; Canada Authority to Proceed March 1; hearing March 6) should stay a criminal/national-security track, not a trade chip—Trump’s February suggestion to mix them drew an immediate walk-back and would trade long-run tech security for a short-run signing ceremony.
key_factors: US tariff leverage intact: ~$250B covered; List 3 10%→25% hike delayed but still available
China showing clearer real-economy stress (PMI contraction, Dec export/import drop, slower 2018/Q4 GDP)
US macro still resilient (sentiment 98.4, VIX ~13.4) — not a recession-from-trade-war setup
Concentrated US cost: soybean/ag retaliation (~90% drop in China soy buys; large unsold stocks)
Talks live but unfinished: purchases easier than structural IP/SOE/currency plus snap-back enforcement
Domestic political constraint against a weak purchases-only deal
Huawei/Meng track is a parallel pressure point that should not be bargained away

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
G20 Buenos Aires dinner: Trump and Xi agree to a 90-day negotiation window. Planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended. Same day: Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou.
Trump tweets that talks have made substantial progress and further delays the scheduled List 3 hike from 10% to 25% (previously tied to the March 1 end of the 90-day window).
Lighthizer and Mnuchin in Beijing for high-level talks. Purchase commitments discussed; enforcement and structural IP/tech-transfer issues unresolved.
US DOJ unseals fraud and sanctions-related charges against Huawei and Meng; US formally requests Meng's extradition from Canada.
University of Michigan consumer sentiment recovered to 98.4 as of 2019-03-01 after a January dip to 91.2.
VIX closed 13.41 on 2019-03-13 — calm risk pricing, not a crisis tape.
US industrial production eased modestly to 102.88 (2019-03) from 103.99 (2018-10), about -1.1% over the window.
US goods imports from China fell from $52.1B (2018-10) to $31.1B (2019-03), a ~40% drop over the window.

Lighthizer told Senate Finance on March 12 that major issues remain unresolved, he cannot predict success, talks may be in the final weeks, and China is pushing for all US tariffs to come off while enforcement is still disputed.
Lighthizer: will not accept a deal without structural changes and enforceability; List 3 hike suspended until further notice; warned a one-shot negotiation will not change all Chinese practices.
USDA chief economist Johansson: China soy purchases down ~22 million tons / over 90%; China fell from top US ag market in 2017 to fifth; farm exports expected down ~$1.9B in FY2019.
China official manufacturing PMI fell to 49.4 in December 2018, first contraction since July 2016; new export orders shrank for a seventh month.
China December exports -4.4%, imports -7.6%; 2018 goods surplus with the US hit a record ~$323B.
On March 1 Canada issued an Authority to Proceed on Meng Wanzhou extradition, keeping the Huawei criminal track live alongside the trade talks.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Stay at the table and work toward a framework that trades large, time-bound U.S. purchase packages (agriculture, energy) and targeted IP/market-access language for a continued freeze of the List 3 hike and a path to rolling back existing Section 301 duties. Do not reopen tariff or hostage escalation, and do not accept a unilateral U.S. snap-back enforcement regime or deep SOE/industrial-policy rewrite as the price of a March summit. Keep Meng/Huawei on a separate legal track while using talks to reduce the chance the United States converts the criminal case into a broader tech blockade.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is material but not existential. Combined U.S. Section 301 coverage is already about $250B of Chinese exports (25% on the $50B Lists 1–2; 10% on List 3), and firm-level targeting is live: the April 2018 ZTE denial order, the 1 Dec 2018 Meng arrest, and the 28 Jan 2019 Huawei/Meng indictments. China’s export engine is already weakening—December 2018 exports fell 4.4% and imports 7.6%, PMI slipped below 50, and official growth talk has shifted to a 6–6.5% 2019 target—while U.S. customs imports from China dropped from $52.1B (Oct 2018) to $31.1B (Mar 2019), about −40%. That maps near the CHN +0.5 anchor (export hit + Huawei targeting) but below it because the most dangerous near-term shock—the scheduled List 3 jump from 10% to 25%—was suspended at the G20 and then delayed again on 24 Feb after Trump cited “substantial progress,” and the original 1 Mar deadline passed without a hike. Action should be mild and deal-seeking, not escalatory: a new tariff or detention move would likely collapse the Washington/Beijing rounds just as Trump is advertising a possible Mar-a-Lago close and as U.S. farm-belt purchases (extra soybeans; talk of ~$30B/year of ag) are the one area where China can move without rewriting the development model. Full concession or formal purchase lock-in is premature: U.S. existing tariffs remain, enforcement and structural IP/tech-transfer/SOE issues are still unresolved, and domestic room for “bowing” is limited. Negotiate—use purchases and limited legal/IP language as bargaining chips, hold the line on snap-back and core industrial policy, and convert the tariff delay into a durable freeze.
key_factors: Section 301 still covers ~$250B of Chinese exports; List 3 remains at 10% after the Feb 24 delay
Huawei/Meng criminal-extradition track plus prior ZTE denial order is a live tech/sovereignty threat
China real-economy stress: Dec 2018 export/import contraction, PMI <50, lower 2019 growth target
U.S. imports from China down ~40% Oct 2018–Mar 2019, confirming demand destruction in the bilateral channel
Talks advanced on purchases/currency MOUs but still gapped on structural reform and enforcement
Trump is signaling deal-seeking (hike delay, possible Mar-a-Lago summit), which raises the payoff to staying in talks versus escalating
